Synthesis of MgO and ZnO NPs
sections.text:
Synthesis of MgO and ZnO NPs The preparation of NPs using plant extracts has several advantages. This reduced the use of reactive chemicals. Chia (Salvia hispanica L.) belongs to the Lamiaceae family of the plant kingdom, with characteristics of an annual herbaceous plant. Chia is well known as a source of oil, protein, dietary fibre, minerals, and polyphenolic compounds with medicinal value, which is consumed as oilseed, flour, whole seeds, and mucilage. The oil content of the Chia seeds with enhanced polyunsaturated omega-3-linolenic acid is the major cause for the increasing interest of the consumers. In addition, Chia seeds are also known for their richness in natural antioxidants such as tocopherols, phytosterols, carotenoids, and phenolic compounds, including chlorogenic acid, caffeic acid, myricetin, quercetin, and kaempferol, which lead to benefits on human health 3 . The presence of these phytochemicals make them biocompatible and useful for in vitro applications because our body does not react against their presence in form of traces left during synthesis if any. After washing Chia seeds multiple times with distilled water and allowing them to dry, we took 3 g of Chiaseeds (Salvia hispanica L.) in 100 mL of distilled water (DW). The mixture was then stirred at 60 °C for 2 h. The aqueous extract was then filtered Fig.  2 . Before synthesizing MgO-NPs, solution A (0.3 M Mg (NO3)2.6H2O) (100 mL) was prepared. Solution A was continuously stirred, and 10 mL of aqueous Salvia hispanica L. (Chia) extract was gradually added drop wise. The resulting mixture was stirred for 18 and 1/2 hours at 70 °C because temperature offers the best balance between the reaction kinetics and precursor stability. 70 °C was chosen as the stirring temperature during MgO synthesis. In addition to facilitate homogeneous nucleation and the development of MgO particles, 70 °C improves reactant solubility and diffusion, reducing fast component evaporation or degradation. It has been demonstrated that well-dispersed and uniform nanoparticles can be produced under these conditions 40 . Yellow residue in the beaker was filtered and calcined at 300 °C for 4 h, yielding the final white MgO nanopowder. The preparation of MgO NPs by the sol gel method is illustrated in Fig.  3 .

 Fig. 3 Preparation of MgO Nanoparticles by sol-gel methods. 
 A schematic representation for preparing the extract of leaves of Dahlia Pinnata plant is shown in Fig.  4 . We chose the leaves of Dahlia Pinnata as they contain bioactive organic molecules and phytochemicals that may reduce the metal ions and stabilize the colloidal particles in the reacting solution 41 , 42  Dahlia leaves were washed two or three times with distilled water. After letting the leaves dry for three hours at room temperature, they were mixed with 100 mL of deionised water to make a paste. The paste was spun at 800 rpm. Room temperature, or approximately 30 °C, was used to create the yellow-colored extract. The extract was filtered using a Whatman filter paper. Eventually, the color of the extract turned reddish brown. 
 Fig. 4 Schematic representation of preparing Dahlia pinnata extract. 
 We uniformly dissolved 3.3 g of zinc acetate dihydrate (ZnC4H6O4) in 50 mL of distilled water in a beaker and agitated it at 400 rpm for 30 min at 40 °C using a hot-plate magnetic stirrer. The solution was stirred for one hour at 80 °C and 500 rpm, and then 20 mL of yellow-colored leaf extract was added drop-wise at a rate of 20 drops per minute. We then gradually added sodium hydroxide (NaOH) to maintain appropriate pH values throughout the process. The white precipitate at pH 10 was oven-dried, mortar-ground into a fine white powder, and calcined for four hours at 300 °C in a muffle furnace. Figure  5  shows the preparation of ZnO NPs using the sol-gel method. 42

sections.heading: Preparation of CQDs from Neem and Rosemary extracts
sections.text:
Preparation of CQDs from Neem and Rosemary extracts After gathering fresh Neem leaves, they wsere thoroughly washed in both taps and then distilled water 2–3 times. After being baked dry at 40 °C in an oven for 24 h, it was crushed into powder. 200 mL of distilled water and 12 g of powdered Neem leaves were mixed well using a magnetic stirrer at 30 °C and 400 rpm for one hour. The resulting extract was centrifuged at 4000 rpm. In Fig.  6 , the CDs were created by a straightforward thermal evaporation method using Azadirachta indica (Neem) extract as the carbon source. We took 200 mL of plant extract into a 250 mL flask and used an oven to irradiate it at 150 °C for six hours. We purposefully used the reaction time of 6 h at 150 °C to improve the process energy efficiency and prevent undue heat deterioration, based on our earlier optimization trials. We used a unique but straightforward method to further improve the synthesis conditions and avoid charring by placing a second beaker filled with distilled water next to the beaker containing the Neem and Rosemary extracts separately inside a hot air oven. This setup is intended to create a saturated hot air microenvironment that effectively balanced the ambient humidity and minimized the thermal stress leading to abrupt charring process. The gentle release of water vapor from the neighboring beaker maintained a controlled atmosphere throughout the evaporation process, ensuring smooth carbonization without any charring. This innovative, cheap and accessible method may provide better reproducibility. The greener processing conditions make the synthesis process effective and environmentally friendly 19 . Irradiation was performed carefully using a hot air oven to prevent spillage. After the product had cooled to ambient temperature, it was centrifuged for 15 min at 4000 rpm to remove larger-sized agglomerated particles. The supernatant containing CDs was collected using a syringe filter. CDs suspended in water prepared using Neem extract were stored at 4 °C. 
 Fig. 6 Preparation of CDs from Neem extract. 
 Dried Rosemary leaves were ground into a coarse powder. Further, 8 g of Rosemary leaves was mixed in 200 mL of distilled water at 30 °C and stirred for one hour at 400 rpm. Rosemary extract (200 mL) was placed in a 250 mL flask and irradiated at 150 °C for six hours in a hot air oven. Irradiation was performed carefully to avoid spills. After allowing the mixture to cool to ambient temperature, the solution was centrifuged for 15 min at 4000 rpm. The supernatant containing the CDs was then collected using a syringe filter. Rosemary extracts CDs suspended in water were kept at 4 °C for storage. Figure  7  shows the preparation of Rosemary extracts CDs. 
 Fig. 7 Schematic flow-chart for preparation of CDs using Rosemary extract.

Introduction Nanotechnology is growing at an exponential rate, owing to the tremendous potential of nanomaterials 1 . Compared to their bulk counterparts, these nanomaterials exhibit significantly improved mechanical, optical, electrical, electronic, magnetic, and physiochemical properties. The remarkable properties of metal oxide nanoparticles, owing to their reduced size and large surface-to-volume ratio, have led to their widespread applications. Therefore, the development of efficient and sustainable nanoparticle synthesis methods and techniques is of increasing interest. High temperatures, energy-intensive procedures, and the use of hazardous chemicals are common in many of the traditional nanoparticle synthesis methods, raising concerns about potential toxicity and environmental effects. Green synthesis has attracted considerable interest as a viable solution for these problems. Green synthesis also referred to as environmentally friendly or sustainable synthesis, involves the use of biomolecules, natural resources, and ecologically safe ingredients obtained from the parts of the plants, e.g., roots, stems, leaves, and seeds. etc 2 . Carbon dots and other nanoparticles have special qualities like large surface area, adjustable fluorescence, and biocompatibility that make them ideal for applications in chemical sensors, electronics, medical diagnostics, and aerospace materials. Their versatility supports innovation in flexible electronics, drug delivery, imaging, catalysis, and lightweight structural elements, contributing to breakthroughs in various technical and scientific domains 3 . Carbon dots (CD) are a broad term for nano-sized carbon nanomaterials, a developing subclass of nanoparticles with a distinctive size of less than 10 nm and quasi-spherical shape 4 . CDs can be prepared using the following methods: solution combustion, co-precipitation, sol-gel, hydrothermal, solvothermal, and thermal evaporation. These methods may employ green routes that use plant extracts 5 . Their production using synthetic techniques poses many challenges for the scientific community, such as the use of dangerous chemicals, significant energy consumption, inability to achieve uniform particle size, restrictions in scalability, and environmental concerns. These elements make it difficult to safely and sustainably synthesize nanomaterials. . Many of these methods are time-consuming, expensive, and toxic to the environment. To overcome these difficulties, researchers are now focusing on eco-friendly techniques. Green nanotechnology provides tools for transforming biological ingredients into environmentally friendly nanomaterials while mitigating their harmful effects. The progress in green chemistry has captured considerable interest, primarily because it is environmentally friendly, safe, and biocompatible 6 – 10 . We have first coated the microtiter plate with 2,5-dimercapto-1,3,4-thiadiazole (DMcT) and then evaporated the nanodots suspended in deionised water. The gradual evaporation of the nanoparticle suspension at 60  0 C for 24 h in DMcT coated microtiter plates leads to the formation of micron size residual ultrathin water film along with nanoparticles suspended in water film and DMcT bound on micro titre plates which finally leads to the formation of unique nano-micro scale dry and stable structures composed of DMcT molecules and NPs as water molecules are gradually removed. The evolution of spinodal wave-like structures as reported in case of evaporating thin films, appears to leave behind spiky and periodic wavy blades and needle-like micro-structures. Being inspired from dewetting of thin films 59 – 66 our efforts successfully yield sharp wavy nano-micro structures composed of NPs and DMcT linking molecules owing to the thinning of their aqueous film via gradual evaporation. The same is confirmed from SEM images. Investigation done on polystyrene surfaces reveals their hydrophobic properties 67 , 68 . Annealing at high temperatures above 110 0  results into the formation of nanostructures, which further enhance its water repellent properties introducing super hydrophobic behavior in it 68 . In spinodal dewetting the instabilities generally evolve with the characteristics wavelength of the order of a few microns proportional to the square of the film thickness 69 . We have devised surface modifications by exploiting the spinodal-like dewetting mechanism using aqueous solution of metal oxide nanoparticles and carbon nanodots. In our study, the presence of nanodots may numerically contribute different energies and pressures, but we intuitively argue that the governing mechanism may be similar to that of spinodal dewetting, giving rise to thermodynamically stable spiky and wavy microstructures with certain periodicity. We critically determine the most appropriate minimum concentrations of nano-MgO and ZnO that can most efficiently inhibit the fungus. For MgO NPs, the maximum coating concentration was found to be 8 mg/25 mL Fig.  17  (a) and (c), while for ZnO, the highest concentration of 8 mg/25 ml Fig.  17  (b) and (d) was found to be the most appropriate concentration that exhibited the strongest inhibition of C. albicans. In case of pure Rosemary extract CDs inhibition is observed for all three isolates. We’ve already explored how nanoparticles and carbon dots can suppress fungal growth, but there’s more to the story. These remarkable nanomaterials unleash a series of additional mechanisms that amplify their antifungal power, further tipping the scales in favor of inhibition. Here’s how they intensify their impact. Zeta potential affects the stability, surface charge, and interaction of nanoparticles with bacterial cell membranes, all of which are crucial to their antibacterial efficacy. Nanoparticles with high positive or negative zeta potential values typically exhibit superior colloidal stability to avoid aggregation and guarantee a wider surface area for contact with microbial cells. Oppositely charged pathogens adhere to the surface of nanoparticles, which prevents their growth and kill them by causing membrane breakdown, intracellular content leakage, ultimately leading to the cell death. Higher zeta potentials of nanoparticles prevent their agglomeration due to electrostatic repulsion, which in turn offers more surface area exposed to the fungal and bacterial pathogens and may enhance NPs efficacy if the pathogens are oppositely charged. Thus, the nanoparticle efficacy against pathogens also depends on the choice of the selection of their pair (i.e. all NPs will not show good inhibition properties against any pathogen). On the other hand, nanoparticles can combine together if their absolute zeta potential is low ( < ± 20 mV), which would decrease their surface area and antibacterial activity. To improve the anti-microbial properties of nanoparticles, particularly in biomedical and environmental applications, it is imperative to optimize their zeta potential apart of wisely choosing them 53 .

These measurements show that nanoparticles typically range from 10 to 30 nm in size. DLS was used to determine the average particle size, size distribution, and polydispersity index, which indicate the variation in particle size within a sample. To determine the stability of the colloidal solutions, the zeta potential was assessed based on the surface charge of the produced nanoparticles. In this study, zeta potential analysis revealed that MgO nanoparticles (NPs) had a significant negative potential value of -32.1 mV. SEM analysis Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was used to analyze the morphologies of the synthesized MgO nanoparticles. We have first coated the microtiter plate with 2,5-dimercapto-1,3,4-thiadiazole (DMcT) and then evaporated the nanodots suspended in deionised water. The gradual evaporation of the nanoparticle suspension at 60  0 C for 24 h in DMcT coated microtiter plates leads to the formation of micron size residual ultrathin water film along with nanoparticles suspended in water film and DMcT bound on micro titre plates which finally leads to the formation of unique nano-micro scale dry and stable structures composed of DMcT molecules and NPs as water molecules are gradually removed. The evolution of spinodal wave-like structures as reported in case of evaporating thin films, appears to leave behind spiky and periodic wavy blades and needle-like micro-structures. Being inspired from dewetting of thin films 59 – 66 our efforts successfully yield sharp wavy nano-micro structures composed of NPs and DMcT linking molecules owing to the thinning of their aqueous film via gradual evaporation. The same is confirmed from SEM images. Investigation done on polystyrene surfaces reveals their hydrophobic properties 67 , 68 . Annealing at high temperatures above 110 0  results into the formation of nanostructures, which further enhance its water repellent properties introducing super hydrophobic behavior in it 68 . In spinodal dewetting the instabilities generally evolve with the characteristics wavelength of the order of a few microns proportional to the square of the film thickness 69 . We have devised surface modifications by exploiting the spinodal-like dewetting mechanism using aqueous solution of metal oxide nanoparticles and carbon nanodots. In our study, the presence of nanodots may numerically contribute different energies and pressures, but we intuitively argue that the governing mechanism may be similar to that of spinodal dewetting, giving rise to thermodynamically stable spiky and wavy microstructures with certain periodicity. Functionalized microtiter plate surface produces thermally stable nano- and micro-sized needles and blade-like structures with ultra-sharp tips and edges. Since the microtiter plates are composed of polystyrene and are designed to be chemically passive, ZnO and MgO NPs, spread on its surface with a tendency to agglomerate. Like-particles attract each other and have a tendency to self-assemble. Figure  14  (c) indicate for the presence of sharp tip needle like structures. The functionalization of surface of microtiter walls with DMcT linking molecules enhances spreading on the surface of the wells apart of giving rise to wavy nano-micro-structures with formation of micron-sized plates with sharp blade like edges. It is used for the identification of the substances as well as their chemical purity. It is an extremely useful technique for confirming dopant incorporation in the host lattice, analyzing lattice disorders, and crystal defects. The nanoparticles and carbon dots have distinctive Raman characteristics. Sharp and distinct peaks are produced by the in-phase vibrations of atoms and molecules in single flawless crystals. High intensity peaks are produced when the scattering from atoms of perfect, ideal crystals superpose and amplify. There are borders and interfaces in nanocrystals. The Raman peaks could be marginally changed by the interfacial phenomena. We see discrete peaks. Impurities produce vibrations that are out of phase and anharmonic, which reduces the intensity. Zeta potential affects the stability, surface charge, and interaction of nanoparticles with bacterial cell membranes, all of which are crucial to their antibacterial efficacy. Nanoparticles with high positive or negative zeta potential values typically exhibit superior colloidal stability to avoid aggregation and guarantee a wider surface area for contact with microbial cells. Oppositely charged pathogens adhere to the surface of nanoparticles, which prevents their growth and kill them by causing membrane breakdown, intracellular content leakage, ultimately leading to the cell death. Higher zeta potentials of nanoparticles prevent their agglomeration due to electrostatic repulsion, which in turn offers more surface area exposed to the fungal and bacterial pathogens and may enhance NPs efficacy if the pathogens are oppositely charged. Thus, the nanoparticle efficacy against pathogens also depends on the choice of the selection of their pair (i.e. all NPs will not show good inhibition properties against any pathogen). On the other hand, nanoparticles can combine together if their absolute zeta potential is low ( < ± 20 mV), which would decrease their surface area and antibacterial activity. To improve the anti-microbial properties of nanoparticles, particularly in biomedical and environmental applications, it is imperative to optimize their zeta potential apart of wisely choosing them 53 .

Conclusion We hope that this out-of-the-box research work proposed on the inhibitory properties of nanoparticles can be very useful in practical scenarios for bio-medical applications. Recently, the world has faced a pandemic situation across the globe during 2019–2023 due to Covid-2019 virus. The world has witnessed that the preventive health care and diagnostic and logistic tools have miserably failed to cover the demand of the world, especially developing countries. The authors hope that the proposed mechanism of anti-fungal coatings and it’s understanding may open the doors for new applications at very low cost in coming future. The work further extends the idea published in recent publication in scientific reports 57  which suggests for the unique reorganization of NPs and QDs owing to the blending of weak dispersion force with that arsing due to NP interactions; a process in which plasmons can play a vital role. A nanodots array can agitate electrons in micro-organisms and may check their growth. That requires more work to confirm, since the process is least understood. Both qualitative and quantitative confirmation of the creation of nanoparticles was obtained through characterization techniques and analysis. We successfully used green method to synthesize MgO and ZnO NPs and C-nanodots. With a particular emphasis on the inhibition of Candida  albicans , this work elucidated the inhibitory characteristics of nanoparticle-coated functionalized microtiterplate surfaces, which can be used for further investigations. The same procedure can be adopted for other pair of pathogens and coating of NPs. This work could be helpful for scientists and researchers working in interdisciplinary areas to further exploit the methodology proposed in this work. In our case studies, we observe the cumulative influence of these factors, because the presence of the DMcT also serves as linking molecule for nanoparticles bringing them closer to form aggregated nano-microstructures. The emergence of sharp tip nano-micro-needles and saw like structures appear to show inhibition properties because of three reasons: (1) high surface to volume ratio and higher density of nanoparticles, (2) sharp tip needle-shaped and blade- like nano-microstructures composed of nanoparticles and (3) interplaying role of zeta potential and interfacial interactions at nano and micro scales. The antifungal properties of metal oxide nanoparticles and carbon dots are currently understudied, indicating a need for more research in this area 76 . The formation of wavy nano-micro-structures with sharp edges as that of blades or even better, can pin down the fungi leading to the significant inhibition. The sharpest blades ever designed have dimensions as low as 3 nm. The metal blades with edge dimensions of with few tens of microns have been designed and are in use 77 . Candida albican fungi have sizes from 5 to 8 µ, typical bacteria have sizes 0.5 -5.0 µ and may have exceptional sizes up to 2.0 cm, and viruses have sizes 5 nm to 300 nm. The atomistic sharp tip needle-shaped nanoparticles and nano-sized saw-like structures with edges of a few tens of nanometres as presented in this paper may indeed contribute to enhance the anti-microbial properties and can be exploited for tailoring anti-fungal, anti-bacterial and ant-vial properties on surfaces. The work is useful for diagnostic, therapeutic as well as for preventive healthcare services. The crystal violet bio-assay technique has already been in use for many decades for diagnostic purposes. Coating of anti-microbial agents on microtiter plates can help to estimate and quantify their doses appropriate enough to use as drugs for fighting against illness caused due to microbial diseases. Understanding such surface efficacy against pathogens may help to devise health care devices used in preventive health care units, which can prevent their growth and check at very early stages. Further finely tuned quantitative and critical study for many other cases may open the Pandora box.
